title: Coupled analysis of arable land input and output intensity using sliding windows
author: Jiang, Ye, et al.

steps.title: Normalize data to 0‑100 range
steps.instruction: Scale both the input‑intensity variable and the output‑intensity variable so that all values lie between 0 and 100.

steps.title: Sort input intensity values
steps.instruction: Arrange all sample values of the chosen input‑intensity variable in ascending order.

steps.title: Configure pyCASW analysis parameters
steps.instruction: Open the pyCASW graphical user interface, select the independent variable (e.g., normalized fertilizer input intensity) and the dependent variable (e.g., normalized staple‑food‑grains output intensity), add the control variables (normalized pesticides, mulching film, agro‑machinery, and labor‑force input intensities) for partial correlation, and set the sliding‑window size w and step width l (example: w = 40, l = 5).

steps.title: Run sliding‑window correlation
steps.instruction: Iteratively calculate the correlation coefficient for successive value ranges of the input intensity.

substeps.instruction: Set the initial window range to [0, w]. Extract all samples whose input‑intensity values fall within this range.
Compute the Pearson correlation coefficient (or partial correlation if control variables are specified) between the extracted input‑intensity values and their corresponding output‑intensity values.
Record the result: use the mean of the extracted input‑intensity values as the x‑coordinate and the correlation coefficient as the y‑coordinate.
Shift the window forward by the step width l (new range becomes [l, w + l]) and repeat the extraction, calculation, and recording steps.
Continue shifting and repeating until the upper bound of the window exceeds the maximum input‑intensity value in the dataset.

steps.title: Visualize and export results
steps.instruction: Click “Calculate” in the GUI to generate a scatter plot of mean input‑intensity (x) versus correlation coefficient (y); colour each point according to its p‑value (≥0.05 black, 0.05–0.01 blue, 0.01–0.001 green, <0.001 red). Then click “Save” to export a CSV file containing columns: ID of value range, x‑coordinate, y‑coordinate, control variables, minimum value in range, maximum value in range, mean value, sample count, correlation coefficient, and p‑value.
